newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - U.S. T-bonds poised to test range bottom.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - U.S. T-bonds poised to test range bottom.

text.p: U.S. September Treasury bonds' next move could be to revisit the bottom of the recent trading range after climbing halfway back from the five-point decline of early August, technicians said Tuesday.

With the Federal Open Market Committee widely expected to leave short-term U.S. interest rates unchanged at today's policy meeting, there is little reason to expect a post-meeting rally if the consensus forecast proves correct, analysts said.
U.S. debt futures were narrowly mixed at midsession, with the September bond up 6/32 at 114-9/32, and December Eurodollars down 1 basis point at 94.15.
If the Fed holds interest rates steady, futures could see a small knee-jerk rally followed immediately by profit-taking pressure, analysts said.
"If they pop them this afternoon, it's probably a fade," said Walter Burke, senior technical analyst for MCM MoneyWatch.
Burke said he looked for Treasury bond futures to remain range-bound between roughly 116-00/32 and 112-00/32 near-term, with the lower end likely to be retested by next week.

Joe Plauche, financial futures analyst for Carr Futures Inc, said the September bond contract either put in an interim top Monday when it reached 114-12/32 or will do so this afternoon before retreating.
That area represents roughly the halfway retracement of the decline from the August 1 high of 116-31/32 to the August 13 low of 111-31/32.
Plauche said he expected the contract to slip below 113-00/32 possibly this week.

Several technical indicators point to a pullback in bond futures, Burke said, among them momentum studies that are now sending mixed signals. Daily stochastics turned upward on Thursday, but the weekly study has been negative since July 21. Getting a trending move is difficult in those circumstances, he noted.
In addition, the most-recent four-week average bullish consensus was 64 percent, much too high to suggest a rally, as is continued call buying interest, Burke said.
